analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from using personal data and surveillance to charge different people different prices for the same product.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has not received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for a company to use "surveillance data"—information about a person's behavior, biometrics, or personal characteristics, including data the company bought—to charge that person a different price for the same product than it charges others. It allows legitimate discounts (senior, veteran, student, loyalty programs) and price differences based on real, disclosed costs, but forbids hidden profiling-based pricing. The FTC and state attorneys general could enforce it, and individuals could sue for at least $3,000 per violation, with pre-dispute arbitration clauses voided for these claims. Airlines and ticket agents are expressly covered, and the bill says federal aviation law does not shield them.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially lower-income shoppers who are most likely to be identified as willing to pay more, would get predictable prices and a legal remedy—$3,000 per violation or actual damages, whichever is greater, with attorney's fees available—when companies use data like browsing history, location, or income signals to set individual prices. Honest sellers who charge everyone the same also gain a more level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful to charge different prices to different consumers for the same product when the difference is informed by surveillance data about the individual.

It lets consumers sue violators directly for at least $3,000 per violation (trebled for willful conduct), and it makes pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for those claims, so consumers cannot be forced into private arbitration.
It gives state attorneys general enforcement power and requires that cost-based price differences and eligibility for discounts be clearly disclosed to shoppers before purchase.
It extends the ban to airlines and ticket agents and clarifies that federal aviation law does not preempt consumer claims over surveillance-based pricing.

analysis.who_pays: Online retailers, airlines, hotels, and any business that uses personal data to tailor prices would lose that practice and face FTC, state, and private lawsuits. Companies selling pricing-optimization and behavioral-data tools would lose a market, since firms whose main business is determining prices are excluded from small-business protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data-driven retailers and pricing software firms

drawbacks.text: The bill would force sellers to move away from individualized pricing toward uniform or disclosed pricing, which the bill's own required small-business study (Sec. 2(e)) implicitly acknowledges could impose compliance costs and constrain pricing practices small firms use.

The private right of action presumes a violation whenever two consumers see different prices for the same product, putting the burden on the business to prove the difference was not surveillance-based (Sec. 2(d)(3)); critics would argue this presumption invites litigation over ordinary price differences like coupons, timing, and channel.

Insurance and credit products are entirely excluded from the ban (Sec. 2(a)(3)), leaving untouched two areas where data-driven pricing can raise costs most—car, home, and health insurance rates and loan pricing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and growing practice—using browsing history, location, and other data to charge individuals different prices—and its private right of action with an unreachable-arbitration clause and attorney's fees gives consumers tools most privacy laws lack. The honest objections: it could force sellers toward a single posted price and away from legitimate individualized discounts, and the broad prima facie presumption shifts a heavy burden onto businesses, which the bill's own SBA study provision acknowledges could burden small firms. But the safe harbors for costs and disclosed discounts blunt the biggest compliance concerns, and the consumer-side gains (predictable prices, no hidden profiling) are substantial.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it, so nothing has happened yet.

narrative.text: Sen. Ruben Gallego introduced the One Fair Price Act of 2025 on December 8, 2025.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; no further action appears in the record.
It has four cosponsors, all Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, no one has gained or lost yet; the outcome currently favors companies that use personal data for individualized pricing, since the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill is stalled

for.name: Sen. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.

for.name: Four Democratic senators (cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors after introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill has not yet attracted Republican support.

industries.industry: Online retailers, airlines, hotels, and other e-commerce sellers using dynamic/personalized pricing
industries.note: They would have to abandon individualized pricing based on surveillance data and disclose the basis for any cost-based price differences. Airlines are explicitly covered by a new prohibition added to aviation law.

industries.industry: Data brokers and adtech firms selling behavioral data for pricing
industries.note: The bill defines surveillance data to include data 'gathered, purchased, or otherwise acquired,' cutting off demand for behavioral data used to set individual prices.
Firms that build individualized pricing tools face a much smaller legal market, and small businesses in that line of work are expressly carved out of small-business protections.

industries.industry: Arbitration industry and firms relying on arbitration clauses
industries.note: Pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers are unenforceable for claims under the bill, opening these disputes to court and class action.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Commerce Committee with four cosponsors and no hearing or markup scheduled. Most consumer-protection bills introduced late in a session die quietly in committee; its chances would depend on the committee scheduling a hearing and on broader momentum around data-privacy or pricing legislation.
